name: Bad frame theory

card.summary: A looksmaxxing idea that a narrow or small skeletal frame (shoulders, clavicles, ribcage) caps how good a physique can look, which shapes how people plan training and leanness.
card.note: A community theory; discussed mainly on forums and contested by other members.

quick.overview:
Bad frame theory holds that some men have a skeletal frame, meaning the width of shoulders and clavicles, the ribcage and overall bone structure, that limits how broad and proportioned they can look however much muscle they add. Believers use it to explain why similar training produces different outlines on different people.

The appearance payoff, for those who accept it, is planning: choosing between building muscle and getting very lean, and focusing on the parts that can change. Other community members argue that most men have a workable frame and that frame varies less than the theory suggests. No published study tests the theory as stated.
quick.how: Practitioners assess frame by eye or by measuring shoulder width against hips and waist, then decide how much emphasis to put on muscle gain, leanness and posture. Discussions typically involve comparing photos of lifters.
quick.risks: The theory has no direct health risk, but forum discussions around it can promote extreme dieting or discouragement. Skeletal structure cannot be changed by training, so strategies focus on muscle, body fat and posture.

lead: Bad frame theory is a concept in looksmaxxing forums that a person's skeletal frame, including shoulder and clavicle width, ribcage shape and bone structure, sets a ceiling on how impressive their physique can look. People who hold the view describe a narrow or small frame as a constraint that muscle and leanness only partly offset. [1]

For those using it, the idea guides what to work on: forum members debate whether to prioritise building muscle, getting lean to show the face, or improving posture, depending on how they judge their frame. [1] The theory is mainly a community concept; no published study evaluates it under this name.

angle.text: Believers use the idea to set expectations and priorities for building the body they want. Skeptics in the same communities argue that most frames are workable and that training still changes the look.

Frame varies little; training still improves the look

paras: In forum usage, frame refers to the skeleton that muscle sits on: shoulder and clavicle width, ribcage size and the overall bone structure. Bad frame theory claims that narrow-framed people look less imposing than wide-framed people even at similar muscle mass. [1]
Users on looksmax.org debate whether frame can be overcome. Proponents of the theory describe frame as unchangeable and some conclude that leanness matters more than extra size.

Another thread argues the opposite: that nearly all men have at least a decent frame, that frame varies only modestly, and that photos of a person said to have a bad frame show a normal one. Contributors there also name professional models they regard as small-framed. [1]

The term appears alongside related vocabulary about bone structure and proportions, and it is one of several concepts used to explain differences in physique outcomes. Posts using it vary between defeatist and pragmatic, with some members stressing leanness and others training.

lore.intro: Frame is discussed on looksmax.org mostly as a fixed trait that shapes physique potential. [1]

claims.claim: A bad frame limits how good a physique can look.
claims.believers: Proponents say narrow shoulders and clavicles cannot be changed and make muscle look less impressive; some suggest getting lean instead, according to forum discussion. [1]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this concept under this name.

claims.claim: Most men have a decent frame, so the theory is overstated.
claims.believers: Opponents in one thread say frame varies only slightly, that photos used as examples can mislead, and that many top models are small-framed. [1]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this claim directly.
